title: The mystery of love
hookLine: love doesn't explain suffering, but it enters it
last: NOT EVEN DEATH SEPARATES US FROM GOD'S LOVE.

lines: MARTHA ON THE ROAD, MARY AT HIS FEET.
cards: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." Two sisters say those exact words to Jesus in John's Gospel. Martha says it on the road.
Mary says it at his feet. It's an accusation and a prayer at once, a sentence grief knows: where were you? You could have stopped this.
Their brother Lazarus has been in the tomb for days. And what he does next is not what anyone writing a neat answer to suffering would have him do.

teach.b: He doesn't explain. Earlier in the chapter, John has Jesus tell his disciples that Lazarus is asleep and that he is going to wake him. He knows how this ends.
Still, when he sees Mary weeping, and the neighbors who came to mourn with her weeping too, the text says he groaned in the spirit and was troubled.
The King James uses the same English word, groan, as Romans 8 two days ago, now for Jesus himself.
Then one question: "Where have ye laid him?" Not why. Where.
Take me to the place it hurts. They say, come and see.
Then the verse that in the King James is only two words: "Jesus wept." The people standing there read it the simplest way: "Behold how he loved him!" That's the mystery.
Christians have offered reflections on why there is suffering, and some readers say none quite closes the question. What the Gospel gives instead is a God who walks into the grief.
John's Gospel opens the same way: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us."
Isaiah said of God and his people: "In all their affliction he was afflicted." Love doesn't stand outside the pain with an explanation. It asks where, and goes there.
This week walked through that: clay jars carrying light, affliction weighed against glory, comfort passed on, darkness that isn't dark to God, the Spirit's groan, love stronger than death.
And today, the center of it: love that enters.

how: Some churches read the raising of Lazarus in John 11 at funerals or in Lent, and churches encourage sitting with the grieving, visiting the sick, and simply being present, as a way of following Jesus into other people's pain.

games.q: what does “the mystery of love” mean?
o: love that enters suffering instead of explaining it
the puzzle of why Jesus waited to raise Lazarus
a secret reason for suffering God reveals to a few

games.q: the mystery of love — tap the pairs.
p: two words in the King James
in all their affliction he was afflicted

s: at the tomb, Jesus explains to Mary why Lazarus died
he asks one question, "where have ye laid him?", and weeps.
in John's telling, Jesus weeps even though he has said he is going to wake Lazarus
he knows how the story ends, and he still weeps with the mourners.
the people at the tomb took Jesus's tears as a sign of love

games.q: you're Jesus. Mary falls at your feet, weeping: "Lord, if thou hadst been here, my brother had not died." the mourners are weeping with her. what do you do?
o: ask where they've laid him, and weep.
tell her to stop crying, because he'll live.
games.why: he groans in the spirit, asks "where have ye laid him?", and "Jesus wept." the explanation never comes. the presence does.

practice: Bring to mind someone who is hurting, notice the urge to explain or fix it or find the bright side, and set that down.

Ask the question Jesus asked, where does it hurt for them, and picture yourself going into that room and sitting down without a speech; if you pray, pray for them simply by name, and if you don't, hold them quietly.
If the one hurting is you and it feels like too much, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

wordCard.voice: The mystery of love. Love that doesn't explain suffering, but enters it: Jesus at the tomb of his friend, asking where, and weeping.

carryVoice: Your line: love enters. At the tomb, Jesus wept. Rest well, and I'll see you tomorrow.
